The word ensign as a noun has a few related meanings. Think of them as a family of meanings connected by a single idea: a symbol that represents something — a country, a military unit, or a rank of authority.
Meaning 1: A Flag (especially on a ship)

This is the most common and important meaning.

An ensign is a flag — but not just any flag. It is specifically an official flag that a ship flies to show which country it belongs to, or which branch of a navy it serves under. Think of it as the ship's "identity card," but in flag form, usually flown from the back (stern) of the ship.

For example:

  • A British navy warship flies the White Ensign (a white flag with a red cross and the Union Jack in the corner).
  • British merchant (trade) ships fly the Red Ensign — a red flag with the Union Jack — sometimes nicknamed the "Red Duster" by sailors.
  • Government and certain official ships in Britain fly the Blue Ensign.

So when you see a large ship out at sea flying a flag at its stern, that flag is almost certainly its ensign. It immediately tells you: "This ship is from this country, and here is what kind of vessel it is."

The word is also used more broadly on land to simply mean an official or ceremonial flag representing a nation, a military unit, or an organization — though the naval use is by far the most dominant.

An ensign is also a rank — specifically, a junior military officer.

In the modern U.S. Navy and Coast Guard, an Ensign is the lowest rank of commissioned officer. Think of it as the starting point — the very first rung on the officer ladder. It is equivalent to a Second Lieutenant in the Army or Marine Corps. A newly graduated naval officer from a military academy, for instance, typically begins their career as an Ensign.

Historically (especially in British and European armies from the 16th–19th centuries), an ensign was a junior infantry officer whose specific job was to carry the regiment's flag (called the "colours") into battle. This was actually a dangerous and honored duty — the flag had to be kept visible and upright even in the middle of combat, because soldiers used it to find their unit and stay organized on the battlefield. So the person trusted with this job had a title to match: ensign, meaning literally "the flag-bearer." This historical use has now largely disappeared, but it explains why the rank and the flag share the same word.
Meaning 3: A Badge or Symbol of Authority (rare, formal)

In its oldest and most formal sense, ensign can refer to any badge, emblem, or symbol that signals rank, power, or membership — such as a king's scepter, a coat of arms, or the insignia on a uniform. You will mostly encounter this meaning in older literature or very formal writing. In everyday modern English, this sense is rare.
How the Three Meanings Fit Together

Even though these meanings look different on the surface, they share a common thread: a visible symbol that says "this is who we are and what we stand for." A flag does that for a ship. A rank insignia does that for an officer. A badge does that for a person in authority. The word ensign captures all of these — a public mark of identity and belonging.
